rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The paper details the preprocessing pipeline used.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Structural neuroimaging data of participants were preprocessed by using the computational anatomy toolbox 12 (CAT12; http://www.neuro.uni-jena.de/cat/). The main preprocessing steps in CAT12 included denoising, resampling, bias-correction, affine-registration, the standard SPM unified segmentation (Ashburner and Friston, 2005), adaptive maximum a posteriori (AMAP) segmentation (Rajapakse et al., 1997), a partial volume estimation (Tohka et al., 2004), and finally normalization by Geodesic Shooting (Ashburner and Friston, 2011) registrations.

The total intracranial volume (TIV) was estimated for each participant, 31 samples with abnormal TIV as outliers (i.e., outside the 1.5 interquartile range) were removed.

rci11_site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The paper states that the residual data did not have any significant site effect after normative modeling, but does not explicitly state that a site effect handling method was applied. It seems the normative model itself is considered the handling method. eMethods 1 provides a t-SNE plot to visually support the claim.
rci11_site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: Instead of the raw grey matter volume data, we used the residual data by referencing to the normative model. In this way, we reduced the variation across data collection sites. To demonstrate this point, we applied the t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) to the grouping features (i.e., the first 5 principal components) to check if the data from different scanners form separate clusters. Indeed, the residuals from the normative data have already reduced the impact of the site effects, as no clear clusters for the data collection sites can be observed. Hence, in our case, the residual data did not have any significant site effect.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: A novel algorithm called random forest with homogeneous canonical correlation (RFHCC) was proposed to identify ASD subtypes. Within each subtype, the association between brain structure deviations and symptom scores was assessed using canonical correlation analysis (CCA).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The study identified four ASD subtypes with distinct brain-symptom association patterns, and this subtyping improved case-control classification accuracy.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using a novel RFHCC algorithm on the ABIDE dataset (1146 controls, 571 ASD), four ASD subtypes were identified with distinct associations between gray matter volume deviations and ADOS social scores. Subtype 1 (n=47) showed positive correlations in frontoparietal regions (r=0.29-0.44). Subtype 2 (n=105) showed negative correlations in midbrain regions (r=-0.20 to -0.31). Subtype 3 (n=110) showed positive correlations in the ventral visual pathway (r=0.19-0.23). Subtype 4 (n=92) showed negative correlations in regions like the anterior cingulate cortex (r=-0.21 to -0.25). This subtyping significantly improved case-control classification AUC from 0.64 to 0.75 (p < 0.05).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The proposed RFHCC algorithm provides a new way to parse the heterogeneity of ASD by identifying subtypes with consistent brain-symptom associations. This could be a step towards precision psychiatry.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The sample size was limited by the availability of ADOS scores in the ABIDE database. The accuracy of mapping small midbrain nuclei could be a limitation for the findings in subtype 2.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The authors provide the Python code for their RFHCC algorithm on GitHub. The study also compares their subtyping method with k-means clustering, showing that RFHCC performs better in terms of both homogeneity of brain-symptom associations and case-control classification accuracy.
